verdict.reasoning: The transcript states the patient is 35 years old: 'Doctor: I'm 35 years old.' The clinician addresses him as 'Peter' and 'him', supporting that he is male.
The patient identifies himself as a lawyer: 'Who likes to be a lawyer?... Yes, of course. I like, I like your work.'

Work is described as okay but with some difficulty: 'I mean, I mean, work is okay. I have trouble at work sometimes. Having headaches, feeling nauseous.' This supports that work is tolerable but associated with some stress/complaints.
There is no mention of smoking or alcohol use anywhere in the transcript, so stating they were not discussed is consistent with the record.

The patient links appetite loss to changing law firm and dates it to about 3–3.5 months: 'That must have started when I changed over to the new law firm... Three months ago. Three and a half months ago.'

Weight loss duration and amount are discussed: 'Roughly six months. Would you say.' Patient: 'Something like that?' and 'Oh, gosh, I would say less than a stone.' The clinician paraphrases: 'So. About a stone? Yeah. Six months. Okay. Okay. Six kilos.' This supports ~6 kg over ~6 months as a close approximation.

The patient describes low mood and energy but hesitates to label it depression: 'I've been feeling down and I didn't really have energy.' The clinician asks, 'Would you say you're depressed?' and the patient replies, 'You never want to say that, do you?' indicating low mood without explicitly accepting a depression diagnosis.

Nausea is present without vomiting or reflux: 'I feel nauseous. Every now and again... You mentioned nausea. Have you been ever sick with it? Doctor: No, actually not.' and 'Do you suffer from acid reflux? Doctor: I do not, no.'

The patient reports normal bowels without red-flag features: 'That's okay. I would say I don't really have problems when going to the toilet.' and specifically denies diarrhea and blood/mucus: 'No, no diarrhea? No.' and 'Okay, so there's no blood in the poo? No mucus, nothing of that sort? Doctor: No, no, just.'

The patient states shortness of breath is not limited to confined spaces: 'It's like when I go into the lift... Is it like in closed spaces? Doctor: No, it happens every time. It happens very significantly in the lift...' He also denies cough and chest pain: 'Any cough? Doctor: No, not really. Just shortness of breath.' 'Do you get any chest pains with it? Doctor: Not really, no... No chest pain.' Palpitations are present in the lift. The claim that dyspnea occurs 'only in confined spaces' contradicts his clarification that it happens every time (though worse in the lift).
He reports headaches and nausea in relation to work: 'I mean, work is okay. I have trouble at work sometimes. Having headaches, feeling nauseous.'
History of hypothyroidism is clearly documented: 'Yes. I had too little activity of my thyroid.' The clinician rephrases: 'Oh, yeah. Underactive thyroid? Yes.'

Stopping thyroxine coincided with the job change about 3.5 months ago: 'I have not been taking it in the last. Actually, since I changed law firm, I would say.' and earlier the appetite/job change timing was 'Three months ago. Three and a half months ago.'
The patient confirms no recent blood tests: 'When was your last blood test? Doctor: Haven't taken one in a long time.' and clinician summarizes: 'Okay, so you've not had a blood test.'

He previously took thyroxine but stopped after job change: 'And in that I took thyroxine.' then 'I have not been taking it in the last. Actually, since I changed law firm, I would say.' which was ~3–3.5 months ago.

No vital signs or physical exam findings are mentioned. The clinician even says no urgent exam is warranted now: 'there's nothing from what you history... that we urgently warrant a physical examination at this point in time.' This supports that none were documented.

While untreated hypothyroidism and symptom timing are discussed, the clinician does not explicitly state that untreated hypothyroidism is 'likely contributing' to symptoms. They say they are 'not quite clear on what picture we are having here' and plan general bloods, so assigning a likelihood is an added interpretation.

The clinician notes lack of energy and proposes general blood tests to look for causes ('we look at things like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels'), but does not explicitly assess fatigue, weight loss, and low mood as 'possibly due to hypothyroidism or another systemic cause.' This differential-style statement is inferred, not stated.

Palpitations and dyspnea are described, and A&E advice is given, but no explicit assessment that they are 'possibly due to anxiety or a cardiac etiology that needs to be excluded' is made. The clinician only labels palpitations and notes emergency criteria, so this etiologic assessment is additional.

Nausea is present without alarm features: the clinician confirms no diarrhea, blood, mucus, vomiting, or significant bowel change: 'You mentioned nausea... Have you been ever sick with it? Doctor: No, actually not.' and 'Okay, so there's no blood in the poo? No mucus, nothing of that sort? Doctor: No, no, just.' They also reassure: 'you've mentioned now your bowels are fine and you're not being sick. So if that's the case, it's okay.'

The clinician orders a broad blood panel including thyroid and other systems: 'we'll just do a general set of bloods where we look at things like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels and your.' Given prior discussion of underactive thyroid, this set implicitly includes thyroid function tests as part of the general workup.

Explicit emergency advice is given: 'Obviously with palpitations or chest pain, if you get. That's more of a medical emergency, you need to go to A and E for that.' and 'If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again.'
The clinician advises monitoring bowel and vomiting changes: 'But if your, you know, bowels change or you're being sick again, you need to get in touch with us.'

The patient is instructed to contact support via the app to arrange blood tests: 'Now, what we need to do is now you need to ring up support... so that we can organize that blood test for you.' and they explain how to find the number in the app.

Follow-up after bloods and possible physical exam is planned: 'Now after we get those set of bloods, we will find out if we can find anything in them. If that's all clear, then we would need to do a physical examination.'

Same as plan-005: 'Now after we get those set of bloods... If that's all clear, then we would need to do a physical examination.' indicates follow-up after blood results for further evaluation and possible examination.
